Example \(1\)

Evaluate the indefinite integral \(\displaystyle \int x^3 + x + 2\,dx\)

Solution

Apply the power rule of antidifferentiation i.e Power Rule

where \(n \neq−1): \displaystyle \int x^n \,dx=\displaystyle \frac{1}{n+1} X^{n+1}+C\)

Where

\( \begin{align} \displaystyle \int x^3+x+2\,dx&=\displaystyle \frac{1}{3+1}x^{3+1} \frac{1}{1+1}x^{1+1}+2x+C\\ &=\displaystyle \frac{1}{4}x^4+\frac{1}{2}x^2+2x+C \end{align} \)


Example \(2\)

Evaluate the indefinite integral \(\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x}\,dx\)

Solution

Applying the natural logarithmic rule of antidifferentiation yields

\( \begin{align}\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x}\,dx&=\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x}\,dx\\ &=ln x+C \\ \end{align} \)


Example \(3\)

Evaluate the indefinite integral \(\displaystyle \int e^{3x}\,dx\)

Solution

Applying the exponential rule of antidifferentiation yields

\( \begin{align} \displaystyle \int e^{3x}\,dx&=\displaystyle \int e^{3x}\,dx\\ &=\frac{1}{3}e^{3x}+C\\ \end{align} \)


Some integrals require rewriting for ease of evaluation. This is demonstrated in the following examples

Example \(4\)

Evaluate the indefinite integral \(\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x ^3}\,dx\)

Solution

The given integral can be rewritten using the law of indices and then applying the power rule of antidifferentiation yields

\( \begin{align} \displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x ^3}\,dx&=\displaystyle \int x^{-3}\,dx\\ &=\displaystyle \frac{1}{-3+1}x^{-3+1}+C\\ &=\displaystyle -\frac{1}{2}x^{-2}+C\\ \end{align} \)


Example \(5\)

Evaluate the indefinite integral \(\displaystyle \int \frac{x^2-4}{x+2}\,dx\)

Solution

The numerator in the integrand is a difference of squares. This can be rewritten as a product of factors i.e \(x^2 −4 = (x +2)(x −2)\)

Therefore

\( \begin{align} \displaystyle \int \frac{x^2-4}{x+2}\,dx&=\displaystyle \int \frac{(x+2)(x-2)}{x+2}\,dx\\ &=\displaystyle \int x-2 \,dx\\ &=\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}x^2-2x+C\\ \end{align} \)
